title: The Untold Pre-History of 9/11
description: As the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks approaches, we should remember that the events of that day were far from unforeseeable. Standing on the 55th floor of One World Trade Center in downtown Manhattan, Assistant Secretary of Transportation Benjamin O. Davis, Jr. gazed upon an audience of government and private-sector security professionals. […]
fullText:
Standing on the 55th floor of One World Trade Center in downtown Manhattan, Assistant Secretary of Transportation Benjamin O. Davis, Jr. gazed upon an audience of government and private-sector security professionals. His subject: the US government’s approach to the relatively recent phenomenon of terrorist hijacking. As the architect of the federal sky marshal program, Davis offered no easy assurances about the escalating threat. Fighting terror, he admitted, presented no quick solutions. Rather, it demanded constant vigilance, because, as Davis noted, “a great deal can be done before a tragedy demands the action that should have previously been taken.” Addressing the solemn room in the North Tower, Davis gave voice to the single greatest fear haunting the aviation industry: an airborne mass-casualty event.

Eight months after he concluded 33 years of distinguished military service, Lt. Gen. Davis—West Point graduate, legendary commander of the Tuskegee airmen, the first African American general in the US Air Force, and the son of the first Black general in American history—now found himself spearheading the anti-hijacking efforts of the federal government. When President Richard Nixon tapped Davis to confront the new and growing threat, the nation was summoning an old pilot for one last journey.

Largely forgotten today, the US government’s decades-long quest to contain and prevent hijackings unfolded in a series of warnings, shifting security postures, evolving threats, and missed opportunities. The attacks of September 11, 2001, which marked the dawn of the new millennium and appeared to many like a wholly new phenomenon, were, in fact, the culmination of decades of changing terrorist tactics, systemic aviation vulnerabilities, and institutional failures to recognize and address known threats.

Domestic air travel in the 1960s was quite different from what we know today. Passengers would arrive at the airport with a ticket in hand, traverse all the way to the departure gate escorted by family or friends, and often walk right onto the tarmac and up a staircase to board the airplane—while facing virtually no screening, identity check, or other security protocols. A considerable number of individuals in the United States took advantage of this situation to hijack airplanes as a means of transport to Cuba or for financial extortion. Because screening procedures were minimal and cockpit access was too often relatively open, these “skyjackings,” as they came to be known, were difficult to prevent. At the same time, a more organized and politically motivated terrorist threat to aviation was forming overseas.

On September 6, 1970, the PFLP launched an operation using two-person teams to hijack four commercial airliners departing for New York City simultaneously. The hijacking of the El Al flight was thwarted mid-air when armed sky marshals shot and killed the male hijacker and subdued his female accomplice. Two other operatives rejected by El Al for that same flight purchased tickets and hijacked Pan Am Flight 93 instead, evacuating the occupants and destroying the plane after landing in Cairo. The hijackers of separate TWA and Swissair flights successfully diverted the aircraft to Dawson’s Field, an abandoned British airbase in the Jordanian desert, where the passengers and crew became hostages.

The crisis then unexpectedly expanded three days later when the PFLP hijacked a fifth aircraft, bringing it to the desert airstrip to extort the release of the surviving El Al hijacker. As the standoff ensued over the next several days, the PFLP demanded the release of numerous terrorists held in several countries in exchange for releasing the hostages. President Nixon recognized the hijackings not merely as security failures but as an attack on the US economy and national security—and determined that the federal government must take the lead.

On September 11, after days of strategizing, Nixon unveiled a sweeping anti-hijacking plan. The measures placed armed federal personnel aboard US commercial flights, expanded airport screening, and accelerated efforts to detect weapons and explosives. They strengthened the collection and sharing of relevant intelligence with airlines and law enforcement personnel.

The commander-in-chief needed a strong, courageous leader to implement this ambitious aviation security program, bound to alter the air traveler’s experience. For this, he turned to Lt. Gen. Davis, who started work on September 21 as director of Civil Aviation Security at the Department of Transportation.

President Nixon meets with Secretary of Transportation John A. Volpe and Lt. Gen. Benjamin O. Davis, Jr., on September 21, 1970, in the Oval Office. (Richard M. Nixon Presidential Library)

Davis immediately began studying other countries’ approaches. His first major initiative was to scale up a sky marshal program to more than 1,700 armed officers protecting commercial aviation in flight. Next, he targeted the airlines’ lax screening and inconsistent implementation of the new federal security procedures. At an international meeting on transportation and security on January 11, 1971, he noted that four recent hijackings could easily have been prevented if the airlines had simply adhered to the new protocols.

In March, Davis went further, urging airline crews to resist hijackers when appropriate rather than simply complying with their demands. This public stance aligned with internal communications between Davis and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator John Shaffer regarding the need to provide special training to air crews to react with force if faced with a suicidal hijacker.

Little remembered today, Davis—“the hijacking guy,” as Nixon and his aides called the general on the White House tapes—became something of a celebrity as he waged parallel campaigns, in private and in public, to raise awareness of the perils of modern air travel. Tall and slender with a trimmed pencil mustache, Davis favored Japanese watches. He appeared as a guest on The Mike Douglas Show alongside Dionne Warwick and Leslie Uggams, obligingly demonstrated new magnetometer devices for newsmen, and drew “roars of laughter” when he related that “One airline told us they handle luggage so roughly that no explosive could survive the loading process.”

Following his initial successes, Davis was sworn in as Assistant Secretary of Transportation for Safety and Consumer Affairs on August 3, 1971. In this role, he spent the next several years working with the FAA, airlines, and airports nationwide to establish a comprehensive Civil Aviation Security System.

Terrorist attacks were becoming increasingly brazen and violent, culminating in the televised massacre of 11 Israeli athletes and coaches at the Munich Olympics in September 1972 by the Palestinian terrorist group Black September. The danger to civil aviation, however, was not limited to organized international terrorism. On November 10, 1972, three men armed with handguns and grenades hijacked Southern Airways Flight 49 shortly after it departed from Birmingham, Alabama, and demanded $10 million. During the ensuing negotiations, the hijackers threatened to crash the aircraft into a nuclear reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory as they circled the facility from above; the 30-hour ordeal ended when the aircraft landed in Havana, and Cuban authorities arrested the hijackers.

The Oak Ridge episode provided the immediate catalyst for a security measure Davis had long urged. On December 5, the Department of Transportation announced that, beginning January 5, 1973, all passengers and their carry-on baggage would be screened before they boarded flights operated by US carriers. The nationwide requirement represented a great leap forward in aviation security and effectively ended the “transport to Cuba” incidents, leading to a major drawdown of the sky marshal program. Hijackings of US commercial flights sharply declined, but the underlying threat to civil aviation did not.

The possibility that terrorists might deliberately crash an aircraft into a populated target had already entered discussions at the highest levels of government. In January 1973, investigative journalist Jack Anderson reported that US officials had warned Israel of intelligence suggesting that the Black September Organization (the covert arm of the PLO) might attempt to hijack an aircraft and crash it into Tel Aviv.

On February 21, Israeli fighter aircraft shot down a non-responsive Libyan passenger plane that had strayed into Israeli-controlled airspace over the Sinai Peninsula, killing 108 of the 113 people aboard. When Prime Minister Golda Meir met with Nixon in the Oval Office on March 1, she explained that Israel had recently received warning that Black September was planning to crash a plane into an Israeli city. Recalling a prior terror attack targeting an airport, she told Nixon that Israel had regarded the unidentified aircraft as a serious threat.

The July 23 President’s Daily Brief (PDB) included intelligence reporting that Israel and Saudi Arabia were both claiming they had information that the hijackers of Japan Airlines Flight 404 were planning to crash the plane in a kamikaze-style raid following takeoff in Dubai. While the Japanese Red Army and Palestinian militant hijackers ended up blowing up the aircraft after its final landing in Benghazi, a potential suicide hijacking scenario had now once again reached the president.

Then, on February 22, 1974, a deranged individual named Samuel Byck attempted to commandeer a passenger plane at Baltimore/Washington International Airport to crash it into the White House. The attempt ended while the aircraft was still on the ground, after police wounded Byck and then took his own life. In a recording sent to Anderson, the investigative journalist, Byck described his plan, dubbed “Operation Pandora’s Box,” to force the pilots to fly towards the White House, kill them, and steer the aircraft into the White House himself. The incident clearly registered with Benjamin Davis.

Against this backdrop, the general joined several other terrorism experts from the FBI, the Department of State, and the private sector on the 55th floor of One World Trade Center for a Conference on Terrorism and Executive Safety, organized by the World Trade Institute on September 11, 1974. In his speech, entitled a “US Approach to Terrorism-Hijacking,” Davis issued this blunt warning to his audience of security professionals:

“Security cannot be left to the judgment of individuals. It must be obligatory at all times, the same as the requirement that an airplane be properly fueled and otherwise airworthy. No one questions the necessity for an effective and dependable navigation and communications system on an aircraft or for a thoroughly qualified flight crew. Security screening is just as important to the safety of the airliner. Since the hijacking virus sprang up in the late 1960s, we have been especially fearful of one specter—a mass air tragedy.”

Davis closed with another warning: that the issue wasn’t going away. “There is an old adage: ‘All that is necessary for evil to triumph is for good men to do nothing.’ We inhabit a shrinking world, interrelated through technology and necessity. It is intricate, a world where cultures and causes often clash…”

As Davis wrapped up his efforts as assistant secretary, he left one final warning for those who would succeed him: “Conventional warfare aside, modern society suffers its cruelest blows from the international terrorist movement. And there is no course for us to take but resistance. Realizing that aircraft and air terminals have perhaps the greatest potential for disaster, the United States must be especially strong in defending those areas.” He then concluded: “And if the job seems too big and too demanding, I can only suggest that we would do well to think of the consequences and alternatives.”

During Davis’ retirement party held at the Fort McNair Officers’ Club on September 11, 1975, Secretary of Transportation William T. Coleman, Jr., the first African American to hold that position, presented his fellow pioneer with the department’s highest award, hailing Davis’ contribution to aviation security:

“I know of no single individual who has made a more effective and valiant contribution to the safety of the traveler. When this decade began, domestic airlines faced the constant threat of hijacking and air piracy. Under the dedicated leadership of General Davis, and against staggering odds, the Federal Civil Aviation System has curbed criminal activity against airlines and facilities.”

In fact, the rate of successful hijackings in the United States had dropped from 33 in 1969 to zero in 1973. Between the time of the imposition of the full Civil Aviation Security Program in early 1973 and Davis’ retirement, not a single commercial airliner from the US domestic fleet was hijacked or destroyed by bomb sabotage.

Although Davis left his retirement party satisfied with what the department had accomplished to date, he knew the threat remained. The aviation security system he had worked so hard to establish continued to evolve over the next several years, with hostage-style hijackings of international flights remaining the prevailing threat. On September 11, 1981, Federal Aviation Regulations Part 108 went into effect, officially mandating that US carriers implement formal, FAA-approved security programs to standardize passenger screening and prevent air piracy.

Alongside these physical security measures, the FAA-approved Common Strategy emerged, which generally instructed flight crews to avoid confrontation, accommodate hijacker demands, and prioritize landing the aircraft safely. This approach reflected a belief that cooperation would successfully bring most hijackings to a bloodless resolution. Yet, this very perceived strength in dealing with a known threat would be ineffective against hijackers whose objective was not political bargaining, but a mass-casualty suicide attack.

That suicidal intent, however, was already appearing in intelligence channels during this exact same window. In August 1979, the Israeli Defense Minister Ezer Weizman announced at a cabinet meeting that Palestinian terrorists were being trained as pilots in Libya for suicide missions to crash planes full of explosives into Israeli cities and that Israel was preparing countermeasures. A year later, US intelligence translated similar regional news reports of the head of the PFLP-General Command claiming the ability to launch kamikaze planes against population centers in Israel.

This rhetoric quickly escalated into state-sponsored threats. A May 1984 Terrorism Review produced by the CIA’s Directorate of Intelligence noted that the speaker of the Iranian Assembly had suggested deploying aircraft on suicide missions against US warships near the Strait of Hormuz. An exhibit entered into the Congressional Record on February 7, 1985 detailed allegations from Iranian defector Houshang Mortezai, who reportedly alerted Western intelligence that he and other pilots were undergoing exactly this type of training for kamikaze-style operations, explicitly including civilian targets.

Similar reports of Syria’s kamikaze pilots had reached the Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) by early June. The June 5, 1985 issue of Early Warning, routed directly to the DCI, quoted Syrian President Hafez al-Assad’s speech at the ninth congress of the National Federation of Syrian Students, allegedly relaying that during his early military career he had discussed with his colleagues the necessity of pilot suicide squads, then continuing:

“Still, we must differentiate between the ordinary mission and the commando [fida’i] mission, which requires the pilot to pounce on the enemy target and strike enemy ships, airports, and other targets by turning himself, his planes, and his bombs into one fireball. Such attacks can inflict heavy losses on the enemy. They guarantee results, in terms of scoring a direct hit, spreading terror among enemy ranks, raising people’s morale, and enhancing citizens’ awareness of the importance of martyrdom.”

The director of the Congressional Task Force on Terrorism and Unconventional Warfare, Yossef Bodansky, later outlined in Target America & The West: Terrorism Today how a former trainee at an Iranian installation in Vakilabad conveyed that one terrorist training exercise involved a Palestinian Islamic Jihad team hijacking an aircraft and utilizing their flight training to crash the plane with passengers aboard into a designated target.

These intelligence warnings about suicide operations emerged in the midst of a wave of increasingly brutal hostage hijackings by Shia fundamentalist groups, including Palestinian Islamic Jihad and Hezbollah, which culminated in the June 1985 seizure of TWA Flight 847 and the murder of a US Navy diver. In response, President Ronald Reagan directed the expansion of the air marshal program on select international flights, which was codified and increased the force to 400 marshals.

Just months later, seven terrorists affiliated with the Abu Nidal Organization attacked the Vienna and Rome airports on December 27, 1985, killing 19 people and wounding about 140 others. A December 30 classified cable from the US Embassy in Rome to the State Department, received in the White House Situation Room, reported that the lone surviving terrorist in Rome told Italian investigators the attackers were suicide commandos who planned to seize an El Al aircraft and blow it up over Tel Aviv. The next day newspapers in Italy and the United States reported that he had described a plan to hijack planes in Vienna and Rome and crash them simultaneously into Tel Aviv.

In early January, the Austrian Interior Ministry announced that its investigation, including interrogations of the two surviving Vienna attackers, had uncovered a similarly described plan to hijack an El Al aircraft, fly it to Tel Aviv, and bring it down over the city in a suicide attack.

In April 1986, the British government caused quite a stir when it expelled 21 Libyan students, including 23-year-old pilot Adel Massoud, who was enrolled at the Oxford Air Training School. This action came after Tripoli Radio broadcast a phone call in which Massoud declared that he and his Libyan classmates in Britain were ready to serve as “suicide squads against America and its arrogance.”

These tensions had arisen following the US bombing of Libya in response to the bombing by Libyan agents of a West Berlin nightclub that killed two American soldiers and a Turkish woman and injured over 200 others. UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher announced in the House of Commons that additional action would be forthcoming regarding over 300 Libyan nationals undergoing training in the UK as pilots or mechanics. White House and State Department spokesmen in Washington welcomed the news.

On December 21, 1988, a different form of aviation terrorism struck when Pan Am Flight 103 exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing all 259 people aboard and 11 victims on the ground. In response, President George HW Bush created a Commission on Aviation Security and Terrorism to comprehensively study and appraise practices and policy options to prevent future terrorist acts against aviation.

The commission’s May 1990 final report determined that existing aviation security systems were seriously flawed, advocated for increased federal leadership, and urged reforms in intelligence coordination, international cooperation, and explosives-detection technology. After Lockerbie, US aviation security policy increasingly focused on changes needed to secure air travel against sabotage, particularly explosives concealed in checked baggage. This focus would shape legislation and institutional reforms throughout the next decade.

In a paper on The Terrorist Threat to Commercial Aviation published by The RAND Corporation in March 1989, Brian Michael Jenkins highlighted “The nightmare of governments is that suicidal terrorists will hijack a commercial airliner and, by killing or replacing its crew, crash into a city or some vital facility.” Shortly thereafter, the ubiquitous Jack Anderson and his colleague Dale Van Atta resurfaced Mortezai’s account of Iranian suicide pilots, also citing intelligence sources to report that terrorist leaders had gathered in Beirut the previous winter and there designated the United States as the prime target.

The columnists warned that terrorists could crash an aircraft into the White House. Contacted by Anderson, President Bush commented: “You’re talking with a man who is old enough to remember the kamikaze pilots of World War II, indeed, whose ship was attacked by such pilots. So I remember it personally and vividly, and I know what damage someone intent on sacrificing one’s own life can do driving a plane.”

World events then took an unexpected turn when Iraqi strongman Saddam Hussein launched a surprise invasion of neighboring Kuwait on August 2, 1990. That September 11, President Bush addressed a Joint Session of Congress, framing the war to come in terms of two major objectives: liberating the United States’ oil-producing ally and making the region, and thereby the world at large, “freer from the threat of terror.” Yet, the deployment of US forces to Saudi Arabia was already deepening Osama bin Laden’s hostility toward the American enterprise. Over ensuing years, these grievances would lead the Al Qaeda founder to identify the United States as the terrorist organization’s principal enemy.

During the same period, the long-retired General Davis continued to warn publicly about terrorist plots against US embassies and domestic targets, and to propose possible safeguards. “The Department of Transportation established this security shield because of the spiraling domestic crime rate and the international terrorist movement,” he reflected in his autobiography published in early 1991. “Terrorism and its perpetrators, after all, are only a jet ride away from this country, if not in our very midst…We are still vulnerable today to the machinations of terrorists, saboteurs, and deranged persons.” General Davis visited the White House on April 23, 1991, and presented a copy to President Bush.

General Davis presents President George HW Bush with a copy of his autobiography at the White House on April 23, 1991. (George HW Bush Presidential Library and Museum)

Still, Yousef, claiming to be a refugee from Iraq, was admitted into the United States without a valid visa pending asylum proceedings. On February 26, 1993, Yousef and an accomplice drove a rental truck containing explosives into the parking garage beneath the North Tower of the World Trade Center. The explosion killed six people and injured more than 1,000 others but fell short of accomplishing its goal of bringing the Twin Towers down. Yousef escaped to Pakistan and continued planning terrorist attacks, this time targeting commercial aviation.

The concept of a commercial airliner being used as a weapon of mass destruction entered mainstream popular fiction in August 1994 when novelist Tom Clancy released his bestseller Debt of Honor that ends with a pilot deliberately crashing a Boeing 747 into the US Capitol building during a joint session of Congress. On September 11, less than a month after Debt of Honor hit the shelves, a despondent Frank Eugene Corder stole a Cessna 150 and, in the early hours of the next morning, crashed it onto the White House grounds. While no fatalities resulted, the event showed these vulnerabilities weren’t limited to fiction. The incident prompted a review of White House security protocols but produced no major changes in aviation security.

Three months later, the possibility of terrorists turning a commercial airliner into an instrument of mass-casualty attack emerged in a far more concrete form. On December 24, 1994, four members of the Algerian Armed Islamic Group seized Air France Flight 8969 in Algiers, murdered three passengers, and directed the pilot to fly to Paris. Nearly 14 hours after the plane landed in Marseille to refuel, French commandos stormed the aircraft, killed the four hijackers, and rescued the passengers and crew. French authorities determined that they likely intended to destroy the plane over Paris, possibly by crashing it into the Eiffel Tower. This event further demonstrated that a hijacked airplane could serve not merely as a means of leverage in hostage negotiations, but as the instrument of lethal attack itself.

Investigators in the Philippines soon uncovered an aviation plot of still greater scale and sophistication. Led by Ramzi Yousef, the Bojinka plot sought to detonate 11 commercial aircraft traveling over the Pacific Ocean to the American homeland. An accomplice, Abdul Hakim Murad, was arrested in Manila in January 1995. The recipient of extensive pilot training in the States, Murad had also discussed with Yousef the idea of a suicide plane attack on CIA headquarters.

Philippine authorities turned Murad over to the FBI and shared the information they uncovered. Following Yousef’s subsequent arrest in Pakistan and extradition to the United States, his uncle, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (KSM), carried the mission forward, specifically by conceiving of a plan that combined aspects of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing and the Bojinka plot. KSM pitched the plan to bin Laden sometime around 1996.

For security officials, it was a time of heightened alarm. On July 17, 1996, TWA Flight 800 exploded off the coast of Long Island. Investigators would eventually determine that an explosion of fuel vapors in the aircraft’s center wing tank caused the crash, but in its immediate aftermath, terrorism was widely feared. Eight days later, President Bill Clinton announced the creation of the White House Commission on Aviation Safety and Security, chaired by Vice President Al Gore. The president directed the commission to produce an action plan focused on advanced explosives detection technology.

On September 11, 1996, just two days after the Gore Commission issued its initial recommendations, Keith O. Fultz of the General Accounting Office (GAO) testified before Congress that “protecting civil aviation from a terrorist attack is an urgent national issue.” Warning of vulnerabilities throughout the system, GAO reinforced the commission’s calls for additional security protocols, including improved explosives detection and passenger-bag matching.

When the vice president issued the commission’s final report on February 12, 1997, it opened with a single word: “Change.” The report recognized that terrorism was evolving and called for a layered security system incorporating enhanced intelligence coordination, vulnerability assessments, employee background checks, access controls, passenger profiling, and defenses against emerging threats such as surface-to-air missiles. The report’s most concrete aviation security initiatives concentrated on preventing explosives from being brought aboard commercial aircraft. As those reforms were being developed and implemented, Al Qaeda’s planners were preparing an operation built around a very different central premise: seizing passenger aircraft and turning them into weapons.

Al Qaeda demonstrated its growing ambition and capacity for the coordination of mass-casualty attacks with deadly bombings carried out at US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania in August 1998. Later that year, General Davis, who had continued to warn about terrorist attacks on US embassies and at home throughout his retirement, made one final trek to the White House. On December 9, 1998, President Clinton advanced him to four-star general in honor of his lifetime of service to the United States of America, with Secretary Coleman, his proud boss during his final year at the Department of Transportation, and 20 of his fellow Tuskegee airmen, in attendance.

That same year, Northeast Air Defense Sector (NEADS) exercises included hijack scenarios that involved suicide attacks on the White House and the Statue of Liberty. The FAA judged this type of attack unlikely, however, reckoning bombing as the primary threat to commercial aviation. Meanwhile, internal FAA audits and other official reviews had repeatedly exposed weaknesses in checkpoint screening, with even obvious test items going undiscovered. At the same time, small knives remained permitted under prevailing aviation security rules.

The arrest of Ahmed Ressam at the US-Canada border in December 1999 disrupted an Al Qaeda plot to bomb Los Angeles International Airport during upcoming Y2K celebrations. Less than a month later, several Al Qaeda operatives met in Kuala Lumpur, including Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, both of whom would later participate in the September 11 hijackings. At the CIA’s request, Malaysian authorities photographed the gathering, and US officials subsequently obtained information about the participants’ movements.

The intelligence community did not effectively track and share information about their movements after they left Kuala Lumpur for Bangkok, and critical data, including Mihdhar’s valid US visa and Hazmi’s January 2000 flight to Los Angeles, was not formally disseminated outside the CIA’s Counterterrorism Center in time for effective action. Over the coming year, the 19 Al Qaeda operatives, all of whom had completed training with Al Qaeda in Afghanistan, continued to filter into the country and move into position to serve their designated operational roles as either pilots or “muscle” hijackers to subdue the passengers and crew.

A suicide attack on the USS Cole, docked for refueling in the Yemeni port of Aden on October 11, 2000, killed 17 US sailors and injured 39 others, further validating Al Qaeda’s asymmetric tactics. Encouraged by their success at Aden, KSM’s plane operation had now evolved from a proposal developed overseas into a mission whose final preparations were occurring largely within the United States.

Although Williams stressed the belief that this was more than a coincidence, no further action was taken. By this point, four of the hijackers, including their ringleader Mohamed Atta, had already completed training at flight schools across the nation. Only too late would it be learned that one of the individuals named in the Phoenix memo was a close associate and flight training partner of Hani Hanjour—who would only months later fly Flight 77 into the Pentagon.

Another general warning came in an August 6, 2001 PDB entry that carried the now-infamous headline “Bin Ladin Determined To Strike in US,” including FBI information noting “patterns of suspicious activity” consistent with preparations for hijackings as well as surveillance of federal buildings in New York.

Ten days later, FBI agents in Minnesota arrested Zacharias Moussaoui on immigration charges. The Bureau had begun investigating Moussaoui, a French citizen trained by Al Qaeda in Afghanistan, following his suspicious behavior at flight training sessions in Eagan, Minnesota. Unaware of the similar concerns raised in Phoenix, the agents in Minnesota were unable to gain approval to search Moussaoui’s laptop and notebook; as a result, his connections to other terrorists remained unknown to the FBI during this initial, and critical, period of investigation.

On August 24—long after both had entered the United States—Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi were finally added to the State Department’s TIPOFF watchlist. As TIPOFF was not integrated into the domestic security infrastructure, both men were able to purchase airline tickets for American Airlines Flight 77 on September 11.

The Federal Air Marshal Program had dwindled to 33 officers assigned primarily to international flights, reflecting a security posture that did not anticipate a threat taking shape within the United States at that moment.

On September 11, 2001, exactly 31 years after President Nixon announced his comprehensive anti-hijacking measures, 19 Al Qaeda operatives cleared airport security and hijacked four commercial aircraft departing from Boston’s Logan International Airport, Washington Dulles International Airport, and Newark International Airport. The computerized prescreening system known as CAPPS selected several of the hijackers for additional scrutiny. Under the rules then in place, however, that selection typically affected only checked baggage and did not trigger enhanced passenger screening. All 19 passed through the standard checkpoints, some carrying knives or box cutters, to board their flights.

At 8:46 am, American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center.

United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower at 9:03 am.

American Airlines Flight 77 hit the Pentagon at 9:37 am.

And at 10:03 am, United Airlines Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew members fought their way into the cockpit and thwarted the hijackers from steering the aircraft back to Washington, DC.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed, and the world was forever changed. That evening, President George W. Bush addressed the nation:

“Today, our fellow citizens, our way of life, our very freedom came under attack in a series of deliberate and deadly terrorist attacks. The victims were in airplanes, or in their offices; secretaries, businessmen and women, military and federal workers; moms and dads, friends and neighbors. Thousands of lives were suddenly ended by evil, despicable acts of terror. The pictures of airplanes flying into buildings, fires burning, huge structures collapsing, have filled us with disbelief, terrible sadness, and a quiet, unyielding anger. These acts of mass murder were intended to frighten our nation into chaos and retreat. But they have failed; our country is strong…”

In the aftermath of 9/11, the United States carried out the most sweeping redesign of aviation security since the Nixon-Davis reforms of the early 1970s. The result was a federally directed, multi-layered aviation security system on a scale without precedent. The Aviation and Transportation Security Act of November 2001 created the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), established a federal screening workforce, strengthened intelligence coordination and information sharing, mandated hardened cockpit doors, and authorized a significant increase in federal air marshals. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 then moved TSA into the newly created Department of Homeland Security, further integrating aviation security into the broader national security framework.

In this sense, these reforms represented the tragic fulfillment of the warning General Davis had issued 27 years earlier when he cautioned at the World Trade Center on September 11, 1974, that “a great deal can be done before a tragedy demands the action that should have previously been taken.”

In their execution and the nature of the threat they posed to America, the 9/11 attacks appeared sudden, new—but they did not arise overnight or without warning. They happened following decades of evolving terrorist tactics and persistent aviation vulnerabilities, revealing the risk that security systems designed to protect against known tactics can become increasingly vulnerable as threats evolve. Twenty-five years after the fall of the Twin Towers and the rise of the black smoke over the Pentagon, we must ensure that vigilance is an ongoing discipline—one that requires us to both remember the last attack and to recognize when the next threat may be taking a different form.

Chris Naylor is a researcher and writer focused on US national security history. He holds degrees in history, German, and public policy from the University of Maryland. title: Mamdani under fire after symbolic 9/11 pen goes to former al Qaeda defense lawyer
description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani faces backlash for handing a 9/11 ceremonial pen to aide Ramzi Kassem, who represented a convicted al Qaeda member.
fullText:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing backlash after giving a ceremonial pen from a 9/11 remembrance ceremony to a top aide who once represented a convicted al Qaeda member whose brother-in-law hijacked the plane that struck the Pentagon.

Mamdani signed executive orders Friday ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, designating the date a citywide day of remembrance and service and strengthening efforts to prevent future terrorist threats.

After signing the final order, Mamdani handed the pen to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and asked her to pass it to chief counsel Ramzi Kassem. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, who pleaded guilty to war-crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships and was the brother-in-law of Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon, killing 184.

Mamdani Faces Growing 9/11 Backlash As Old Post Resurfaces Ahead Of Ground Zero Ceremony: 'Is This Real?'

The handoff drew criticism on social media, with users arguing on X that Kassem's role in the ceremony distracted from an event meant to honor those killed in the attacks and the first responders who died trying to save them.

"This is a slap in the face to victims ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11," wrote podcaster Benny Johnson on X.

Flashback: Mamdani Torched For Recycling 9/11 Tributes After Years Of Near-identical Posts

"I sincerely hope the rest of the country understands just how hard it is to be in New York City with this mayor, and especially as we're approaching this most serious and solemn day for NYC: 9/11," wrote former New York state Senate candidate Maria Danzilo.

Another user on X called it a "deliberate gesture by Mamdani that undermines 9 / 11 yet again with impunity."

Accused 9/11 Mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, 3 Co-defendants Set For 2028 Trial

City Hall told the New York Post that Kassem attended the ceremony because he and his team drafted both executive orders as part of his duties as chief counsel.

That role has drawn scrutiny because Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, a Guantánamo Bay detainee who pleaded guilty to war-crime charges tied to al Qaeda plots against commercial ships, including the 2002 bombing of a French oil tanker off Yemen's coast. Al-Darbi's sister was married to Khalid al-Mihdhar, one of the hijackers aboard the plane that crashed into the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001.

Kassem also founded a CUNY legal clinic that provides free representation to Muslims and represented Mahmoud Khalil, a leader of the pro-Palestinian encampment at Columbia University who was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: New York City pausing some AI tools in schools
description: New York City imposes a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI tools for grades K-8, citing concerns about youth mental health.
fullText:
“A six-year-old child is too young to slice an onion, to fry an egg or to use a stove safely. But once that child becomes 16, that knowledge becomes something they are mature enough to learn,” stressed New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani, while announcing a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students.

In what has been described as one of “the most expansive student-facing AI policies in the country”, the Mayor and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels on September 2 imposed a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI for pupils up to eighth grade for the 2026–27 academic year.

Here’s what you need to know about the moratorium, why NYC introduced it, and why the move could set a global precedent.

This move will affect nearly 6,00,000 public school students across the United States’ largest school district. Companion chatbots will be prohibited across all grades, while the AI components of more than 38 previously approved programmes that fail to meet the new standards will be disabled or discontinued.

However, not all AI has been banned. Teachers can continue to use approved tools for planning and administrative work. Assistive technologies required by students with disabilities, as well as certain AI tools used in career-readiness programmes, remain permitted where necessary and under the policy’s safeguards.

Five limited AI pilots will also operate throughout the year for high school classrooms. These select tools are Quill (15 minutes per week) for English language arts; Edia (20 minutes per week) for mathematics; Brisk Teaching (10 to 20 minutes once or twice weekly) for teacher-created activities; Playlab (two assignments per marking period; 45 minutes per week) for assignment-specific applications; and Intel AI-Ready Schools (one period per week) to assist students in identifying community issues and developing solutions through term-long projects.

Every high school student will complete two 45-minute modules per year aimed at developing critical thinking around AI use, including its risks, limitations, and scope. Alongside AI restrictions, tighter individual screen-time limits have also been introduced. Children from 2-K through to second grade will have no routine screen time. For those in grades three to five, NYC Public Schools recommends no more than 30 minutes a day of individual screen use; for grades six to eight, the recommendation is 45 minutes. These restrictions do not prohibit teacher-led use of computers, tablets, or interactive whiteboards during lessons.

Throughout the academic year, a panel comprising students, educators, parents, elected officials, union partners, and field experts will assess the impact of the moratorium and pilots, delivering a report with policy recommendations in April 2027.

“Children need teachers and human connection in order to learn and grow,” Mr. Mamdani said. “They need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with educators, and wrestle with tough problems on their own.” Mr. Samuels also made a similar argument. Learning, he said, involves getting something wrong, trying again and eventually getting it right. That struggle is not an inconvenience that technology should eliminate; it is part of the learning process.

This move arrives amidst growing concern over screen time harming youth mental health. Studies have linked excessive scrolling, social media exposure and reliance on AI in children to lower critical thinking abilities, shorter attention spans, anxiety, and depression. While evidence connecting AI chatbots to suicide risk remains limited, several cases have prompted lawsuits alleging that interactions with chatbots contributed to young people’s deaths. Mr. Mamdani’s decision follows OpenAI’s launch of a teenage version of ChatGPT on August 18 featuring parental controls and content restrictions regarding self-harm and suicide. On August 26, Meta similarly announced stricter time limits, night-time blocking, and muted notifications during school hours for teenage accounts on Instagram and Facebook.

“The tech industry wants us to believe that AI-powered early education is not only inevitable but necessary. We do not see it that way,” Mr. Mamdani added.

Research supports a cautious stance. A 2026 CEPR discussion paper by researchers at Stockholm University and the University of Hong Kong examined more than 26,000 students in China over 30 months. They found that access to generative AI increased homework scores by 18% and reduced completion time by 30%. However, after roughly six months, the same students’ closed-book examination scores had fallen by 20%. A broader review by the Brookings Institution’s Centre for Universal Education, analysing over 400 studies and interviews with 500 educators and pupils across 50 countries, concluded that the potential harms of generative AI in primary and secondary education currently outweigh the benefits—though tailored applications with proper safeguards can enrich learning.

How are other parts of the world dealing with a similar dilemma? The United Arab Emirates is moving towards more structured AI education, rather than a moratorium. It has announced an AI curriculum across public and private schools covering areas such as data, algorithms, applications, risks and ethical use. It also plans to train about 22,000 educators in using AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis and lesson planning.

Norway has adopted a more cautious approach. Its education authorities have recommended that pupils in grades one to seven should not be given access to generative AI, while students in eight to 10 should be introduced to it gradually.

Australia has taken another route: a national framework for responsible and ethical use of generative AI in schools, rather than a blanket prohibition. The European Union, meanwhile, has sought to regulate high-risk uses of AI. Under the EU AI Act, certain systems used in education — including those involved in evaluating learning outcomes or determining access to education — can fall into the high-risk category. The legislation does not amount to a general ban on generative AI in schools.

Poland is going further in the opposite direction, investing almost 1.9 billion zloty to equip 12,000 schools with AI laboratory sets as part of its broader digital education push.

And where does India stand? India is closer to the integration camp. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 identifies artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies as important to India’s changing educational and employment landscape, and calls for contemporary subjects such as AI to be introduced at appropriate stages, alongside greater emphasis on computational thinking.

The Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE) introduced Artificial Intelligence as an optional sixth subject in Class IX from the 2019-20 academic session. More recently, for 2026-27, CBSE launched a dedicated Computational Thinking and Artificial Intelligence curriculum for Classes III to VIII, with AI and allied-subject curricula for Classes IX to XII also finalised. The curriculum emphasises logical reasoning, pattern recognition, algorithm design, data literacy and responsible and ethical AI use.

fullText:
Affordable, fast-heating and with a clever air fryer function, this versatile model is a winner for outdoor cooks who are willing to give up the traditional flame

The best pizza ovens – tested

 Gozney Dome Gen 2 pizza oven review

An electric pizza oven with no flame and no need to rotate the pizza may seem sacrilegious to purists, but the Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven solves many of the hassles of outdoor pizza making. There’s no lighting or monitoring a flame, no need to keep adjusting the heat, and no need for a turning peel, bulky gas bottle or constant use of an infrared (IR) thermometer (although you may still want one – read on for details).

Equipped with four presets – Artisan, Thin Crust, New York, Pan – plus a custom setting to enable you to bake your pizza exactly how you like it, the Ninja Artisan is as effortless as can be, even next to the simplest plug-and-play gas oven. As you might expect from Ninja, it’s a multipurpose cooker, too, transforming into an outdoor air fryer with a capacity to turn out up to 1.3kg of french fries, or bake six chicken breasts.

Being electric also means fast heat-up – useful if a rain shower is looming. In tests, it reached 370C in 14-15 minutes, and pizzas were perfectly cooked in just two minutes, despite the three-minute preset. At an RRP of £314.99 (but £229.99 at the time of writing), it costs about the same as a compact gas oven but is cheaper to run, using less than 1kWh of electricity after an hour at full temperature.

I tested the Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven & air fryer MO201UK in the same way I test all pizza ovens I review for the Filter, although the temperature range here is different.

As well as judging the quality of pizzas cooked with different toppings – cheese and tomato at 370C; a veggie pizza with onion, pepper and tomato at 220C to slowly caramelise the toppings; and a salami pizza at 245C – I rated the oven for ease of assembly, overall usability, temperature control and how easily it could be stored.

I also recorded how long it took the oven to heat up to its maximum temperature of 370C (which is lower than the maximum on gas and wood-fired ovens).

Those with gas or wood-fired ovens are likely to need to plan pizza nights, ensuring they have enough fuel and that the weather will hold out long enough for both the oven heat-up and the cooking time.

With the Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven, you can be more spur-of-the-moment. Simply plug it into an outside socket, and heat-up is fast, with a beep to signify it’s ready to use. And because there’s no flame and the heat is evenly distributed, there’s no need to even rotate your pizza mid-cook.

You’ll need to keep a close eye on cooking time, however. I was caught out with my first pizza, so I shortened the cook time for the next. The Artisan’s door also takes some getting used to: unlike standard open-fronted pizza ovens, you’ll need to factor in time to open it to check or remove your pizza before the base or crust starts to char. Every second counts.

Dimensions: 40.31 x 57.2 x 31.39cm (WDH) / mouth 34 x 12cm (WH) 
Running cost for one hour on maximum: 25p (£0.25/kWh x 0.989kWh; 15-min heat up, 45mins at 370C)
Maximum capacity: 30 x 31cm pizza stone (working capacity 12in pizza) 
Features: four functions: Pizza, Bake, Air Fry & Prove; 30cm sq bake tray, pizza peel, air-fry basket

 Fuel: electric, 1,760W

 Dishwasher safe: no
Spare parts: replacement stones, base unit, bake tray, air-fry basket
Weight: 13.98kg

Beyond its preset programmes and ability to cook more than pizza, the MO201UK Ninja Artisan electric outdoor pizza oven’s standout feature is its rapid heat-up time. It reaches 370C from cold in just 14-15 minutes, giving you just enough time to shape your dough and add your toppings. While it’s faster than a gas pizza oven, it’s worth noting that gas ovens typically cook at a higher temperature of about 430C.

But it’s quick to cook, too. While a thin, lightly topped pizza typically takes about 90 seconds in a gas-powered oven, the Ninja’s Artisan programme is set to three minutes. In my tests, though, I found two minutes was enough. The full three-minute cook burned my pizza, whereas reducing the time produced a well-risen crust with just a slight char on one edge.

For a slower cook, choose the New York setting, which runs for eight minutes. This produced a pizza with browned meat and a reasonable rise, without any burning.

The Ninja Artisan’s tightly sealed door helps the oven retain heat (and makes it safe to use), but it can also be a barrier to the best results. I found it stiff and difficult to open single-handed – with my pizza peel at the ready in the other hand – which made it tricky to launch the pizza and resulted in some burning as I struggled to retrieve it once cooked. Hopefully, the door loosens somewhat with use.

A more concerning issue arose when switching from high- to low-temperature cooking. After making pizza at 370C, I selected the 220C Pan setting for a veggie pizza. Although the oven beeped that it was ready, the stone was still far too hot for a 13-minute cook. Because of this, if you’re likely to switch temperatures often, I’d suggest having an IR thermometer to hand so you can check that the stone is at the right temperature before adding your food.

Once at the lower heat, the Artisan appeared to have cooked the veggie pizza well – although on trying to remove it, I found it had stuck to the stone, which reinforces the earlier point of the temperature not being right after all. As such, it might be wise to do your lower-temperature cooking first, and know that the heat is accurate, before ramping up to the hottest settings.

As an outdoor electrical appliance, the Ninja Artisan comes with a shorter warranty than most gas pizza ovens: one year as standard, extended to two years if you register it with Ninja. Spare parts, including the base unit, pizza stone and air-fry basket, are also available.

Note, too, that while Ninja says the Artisan electric pizza oven has been built to withstand outdoor elements, it recommends buying a cover for “extra protection”. There’s also extensive cleaning and care advice for prolonging the oven’s lifespan.

The MO201UK Ninja Artisan pizza oven has plenty going for it compared to other such appliances. It’s relatively affordable, heats up faster than a gas-powered model, allows for spur-of-the-moment pizza making, and is “plug and play” – no gas, wood or charcoal required. From a convenience point of view, it’s hard to beat.

Its ability to bake and air fry foods will also appeal to outdoor cooks. There’s no need to keep popping inside to your kitchen for chips, chicken, nachos or sweet treats; you can do it all in the Ninja Artisan (with recipes for everything from a tart to cookies and granola included).

There are compromises, however. While the pizzas are very good, they lack the blistered finish you’d get from hotter temperatures. The Artisan’s door also creates issues, making it trickier to launch and retrieve pizzas compared with open-mouthed ovens. And while electric power is undeniably practical, I missed the charm of cooking over a live flame.

Whether the MO201UK Ninja Artisan is right for you will depend on what you want from an outdoor oven. If versatility, convenience and cooking a range of dishes for family and friends are top of your list, the Ninja Artisan is an excellent choice. But if you want to master the perfect leopard-spotted crust, manage a live flame and turn out pizzeria-quality margheritas, a traditional gas oven (such as my overall favourite, the Gozney Arc Lite) still has the edge.

fullText:
NEW YORK — It's probably fitting that in the world's economic and marketing capital, a Grand Slam tennis tournament doubles as one giant product-placement opportunity.

Little-known players who play on stadium courts end up with last-minute patches stuck onto their kits. Their lesser-known coaches wear hats from brands such as the IT company Infosys and the used-car retailer Carvana.

The week before the U.S. Open is a strange mélange of tennis-related activations. Aryna Sabalenka appears at a Brooklyn Heights pizza joint to promote an energy drink. The Waldorf Astoria puts a tennis court in its famed ballroom for an exhibition with Tommy Paul, Maria Sakkari, Ben Shelton and Leylah Fernandez to promote its new global racquet club venture. Jannik Sinner, injured and back home, chimes in from afar on social media, saying he misses everyone at the U.S. Open, including "@baccarathotels and the whole team who always makes me feel at home."

As the field gets winnowed down and all but the biggest stars and some supporting characters remain, there's a pretty good chance tennis fans might scratch their heads and wonder why so many coaches are wearing swag with one of two or three ubiquitous logos.

One of the most prominent is Eight Sleep.

The company makes high-tech mattress covers that users can heat or cool to their desired temperature. The product tracks sleep patterns and measures users' quality of rest. It is not to be confused with IM8, the nutritional supplement company co-founded by David Beckham.

IM8 has Sabalenka as an ambassador. Her coaching staff has worn IM8 swag, though things can get confusing because her coach, Anton Dubrov, is now part of the Eight Sleep team.

Sabalenka, the two-time reigning champion and world No. 1, plays most of her matches in Arthur Ashe Stadium and many of those in primetime. The camera often shifts to her coaching box. That's a lot of airtime for Eight Sleep, even though Sabalenka does not directly endorse the company.

Dubrov does. So does Frédéric Fontang, who coaches Jiří Lehečka, and Michael Russell, who coaches Taylor Fritz, and Jamie Delgado, who coaches Grigor Dimitrov.

On Russell, the logo for Eight Sleep has to fight for attention, since Russell is the closest thing tennis coaching has to a NASCAR driver. He wears patches from Waterdrop and Solinco. Hats from Eight Sleep and Papatui, a men's skincare brand founded by Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson. Sometimes, Russell wears a Carvana shirt.

Carvana is another of the logos that are everywhere at this U.S. Open — it's on the coaching teams of Amanda Anisimova, Madison Keys and many more.

Alexandra Zatarain, a co-founder of Eight Sleep, said the company has worked with athletes, including Fritz, but these days it often makes more sense to work with their coaches.

They are the ones who set a player's routine, working with a nutritionist on what they eat, and with a physiotherapist and fitness trainer to plan the athlete's preparation and recovery, practices that have become far more complex over the last decade. Optimizing sleep is a big part of that.

"We had this idea of just, 'Oh, what if we make the coaches our partners because they are actually a really important partner in making sure that the player stays on track in terms of all of their health,'" Zatarain said.

And, fortuitously for would-be sponsors, something happened in tennis that made these arrangements even more appealing. Coaches are allowed to coach more openly. They don't have to speak with hidden signals, like removing a hat when they want a player to serve wide or standing and clapping when they want the player to move closer to the net.

In 2022, the U.S. Open launched a trial that allowed off-court coaching during matches for the first time. The other Grand Slams followed the next year. In 2025, World Tennis, the sport's world governing body, changed the rules, allowing it essentially everywhere.

The interplay between players and their coaches often generates some of the most dramatic viewing moments of a tennis match. So, the camera finds them — a lot.

"The coaches, I think, are getting a little bit more visibility," Zatarain said.

Their jobs have also changed in recent years, as teams have grown and coaching a top player has become a sophisticated operation. In the best and most serious environments, it's something like being a chief operating officer of a Formula 1 team, where the player is the car.

Enter the relationships with companies that seek to improve the health of people who may or may not compete in sports. There are only so many tennis players who care about what kind of strings a coach and player might prefer. But everybody sleeps. And a lot of people take energy supplements, including just about every player on tour.

"It's like a holistic approach," Fontang said,  "with clear goals, a clear process and to something that you do consistently right as well in the process. This is how you bring consistency into the match."

Fontang played on the tour in the 1990s, which is now considered a prehistoric era in terms of recovery science. He did a little stretching and mobility work before and after he played. Occasionally, he might get attention from a tour trainer or physiotherapist. He certainly didn't have one on his team.

Ivan Lendl, a star of the 1980s, was the first major men's player known to focus on health and wellness. Martina Navratilova was the first woman.

They both won a lot. Other players noticed.

Now, everything is tracked. Blood gets tested to monitor training and recovery. Nearly everyone rides a stationary bike — high tension, low speed — after a match and quickly downs a protein recovery drink.

And therein lies the opportunity. What separates the Eight Sleeps and IM8s and Solincos of the world is that they have an actual use in the sport, compared with a random resort company that just uses a coach as a billboard. A couple of years ago, Fritz had Eight Sleep install a mattress pad in his hotel room in New York.

Nearly every player goes through a sophisticated recovery routine, but the common denominator is the most valuable recovery activity of all.

"Sleep is the first thing that is the most important," Dubrov said after a late match — a common occurrence at the U.S. Open. Everything else will get cut short so that Sabalenka can maximize the amount of time she can spend in bed, though quality can count as much as quantity.

The hot European summer was not great. There isn't much air conditioning in London homes.

"You can have like 10 hours of the sleep," Dubrov said. "But you're going to be kind of awake for most of it."

Russell said he was introduced to Eight Sleep by Fritz, who has long had sleep issues because he can spend a lot of time playing video games. As a teenager, he got in trouble with USTA coaches because he was often gaming until 4 a.m. It's healthier than clubbing, but still not great.

His team noticed improvements in his sleep data in recent years. Maybe it's his mattress pad. Maybe it's a placebo effect, which Russell calls "the most powerful drug there is."

And a clear branding opportunity, present even as Fritz lost Saturday in five sets to Argentina's Francisco Cerúndolo.

So, no matter who advances to the second week of this marquee tournament, expect plenty more sponsorship and caps that look like they could be plentiful at company retreats.

fullText:
NEW YORK — For years baseball people have marveled at the Tampa Bay Rays' ability to remain competitive in the American League East despite consistently low industry payrolls and annual attendance. Since 2008, the Rays have been to the postseason nine times, including the World Series twice, always with payrolls of well over $100 million less than the Yankees.

At the same time, Tampa Bay fans have gotten used to the Rays' jettisoning their favorite players (See: Isaac Paredes, Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe and Tyler Glasnow in just the last three years) as soon as they became too costly or near free agency. And with the clock continuing to tick on their expiring (2028) lease at dreary Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla., there's never been a sense of permanence of the Rays in Tampa Bay.

Recently, both the Tampa city council and the Hillsborough County commissioners voted to approve a new $2.3 billion mixed-use stadium project near Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry Boulevard campus, not far from Raymond James Stadium, the home of the NFL Tampa Bay Bucs. The plan is similar to what the Atlanta Braves constructed in Cobb County, Ga., in 2015 for a stadium surrounded by a village of shops and restaurants that would produce addition revenue for the team.

It was always the accepted view of most folks in the Tampa Bay area that if the Rays were going to survive they would have to be in Tampa where the large majority of their 3 1/2 million residents are. This was part of the reason the Rays have remained one of the top revenue sharing recipients in baseball, an average of nearly $60 million a year. That's on top of the $50 million they and the other 29 clubs receive annually from the MLB Central Fund. So they've had the money to increase payroll, but the previous Rays owner Stu Sternberg just chose not to spend it.

If the owners are able to establish a cap in the new collective bargaining agreement, revenue sharing would go away, but the Rays are anticipating revenues of far more than $60 million from the new park and surrounding village which is now slated to be ready by 2029. For sure, now that the stadium issue has finally been resolved, the Rays, under their new ownership led by Jacksonville developer Patrick Zalupski, are expected to be operating vastly different. Last week Zalupski told the Tampa Bay Times: "Tampa's the No. 11 media market in the country. There's nothing holding it back, "adding that with the new ballpark and the development around it, "we should be able to drive payroll (currently 27th at $116,208,358) into the top 15 circle and maybe even the top 10."

In the meantime, the Rays have been leading the American League East since June 27, but will be facing their biggest challenge now in the September stretch, starting with this present road trip through Texas where they snapped a 10-game skid at Globe Life Field as of Friday, and three in Atlanta against the Braves. They then finish the season with three games with the Red Sox, four in New York with the Yankees and three more at home with the Phillies.

That four-game series at Yankee Stadium Sept. 22-24 figures to be the biggest regular-season series for both the Rays and the Yankees in years, especially since the Yankees expect to be (Aaron Judge) whole, while Rays GM Eric Neander made significant upgrades to his pitching at the trade deadline with Freddy Peralta from the Mets and hard-throwing righty reliever Tyler Wells from the Orioles, and in perhaps the best acquisition of all, filled the Rays longstanding need — a catcher who can hit — by landing Liam Hicks from the Marlins

If the Rays are able to emerge through that gauntlet still atop the AL East it should be cause for considerable concern for the Yankees. Because as improved as they've become this year, they figure to be this good and better for years to come with one of the top player development systems in baseball with a half dozen top 100 prospects including outfielders Theo Gillen, Jake Melton and Austin Overn and catcher Caden Bodine, all of whom could be making their debuts at some point next year.

In every way, the baseball future couldn't be brighter in Tampa Bay.

title: Giants’ DJ Reader Gets Blunt on Pressure to Replace Dexter Lawrence
description: The New York Giants made the tough decision this offseason to replace one of their best and longest-tenured players, defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence.After seven seasons, three Pro Bowl nods, and two second-team All-Pro honors, the former 17th overall pick and the team that drafted him were unable to find common ground on an extension, and […] The post Giants’ DJ Reader Gets Blunt on Pressure to Replace Dexter Lawrence appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The New York Giants made the tough decision this offseason to replace one of their best and longest-tenured players, defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence.

After seven seasons, three Pro Bowl nods, and two second-team All-Pro honors, the former 17th overall pick and the team that drafted him were unable to find common ground on an extension, and the Giants traded him to the Cincinnati Bengals, netting a first-round draft pick.

To replace him, New York turned to the free-agent market, inking veteran names like DJ Reader and Shelby Harris to replace Lawrence in the aggregate.

It's never going to be easy replacing a former All-Pro-caliber player, but Reader told the New York Post's Steve Serby he's going to do his best despite his different skill set from Lawrence.

In the interview with the New York Post, Serby asked Reader about the pressure he's facing in replacing such a talented player on the New York Giants, but the 10-year veteran is ignoring the outside noise and focusing on himself.

"I put a tremendous amount of pressure on myself as a player, especially in the run game. Obviously there's pressures from the outside, but I don't pay attention to 'em as much. I feel very confident in me being to do the job I came here to do. Not gonna be that player, not looking to be Dex, he plays the game a little bit different than the way I play it, but I feel like we both do it effectively," Reader told Serby.

"We affect the game. We affect the quarterback, we affect the run game. The thing is a special way that I do it, and I've been doing it for a long time at a high level in my position. So I would just say you're getting a physical player who's really bought into the system and is gonna play his ass off."

While Reader is certainly a great player in his own right, he doesn't have the career accolades a player like Lawrence has to his name. That doesn't mean he can't be impactful, though, and in some areas on defense, the former Detroit Lions defensive tackle is actually better.

Lawrence was an elite pass rusher for the New York Giants over the last seven years of his career. He recorded a grand total of 30.5 sacks, which is a lot for a defensive tackle.

But he always seemed to struggle against the run, which has been the Giants' biggest defensive weakness over the last few seasons.

Just last season, New York gave up 145.3 rushing yards per game, 31st-worst across the entire league.

Reader, who carries a reputation as a staunch run defender, is hoping to change that in 2026.

Serby asked the veteran defensive tackle if the Giants will be able to stop the run this season in the interview, and Reader gave a short but stern answer.

"Yeah, I confidently believe so. We gotta go out there and do it, but I believe so."

We'll see if Reader and Big Blue's new-look defense can pull it off.

title: Ex-NFL agent: Giants RB Cam Skattebo's margin for error is shrinking
description: A former NFL agent believes the representatives of New York Giants RB Cam Skattebo must step in and save him from himself.
fullText:
The New York Giants are entering the 2026 NFL season with a running back room that has a little bit of everything. They have experience, depth, toughness, and versatility.

That is, if everyone can stay healthy and focused.

Which brings us to the case of second-year back Cam Skattebo, who became a folk hero last year in just eight games. Skattebo, a fourth-round pick out of Arizona State, suffered a fractured ankle midway through the season, but not before capturing the hearts and imagination of Giants fans.

His smashmouth style and straightforward approach to the game and life in general may not support a long NFL career. People are taking notice, most notably Giants' head coach John Harbaugh.

"Skatt's great. He does bring a lot of energy," Harbaugh said last week after Skattebo started a skirmish with defensive players at practice.

"But he did get a 15-yard penalty at the end of practice. Did you notice that? That's not infectious. Well, it is infectious, actually. Infectious in a bad way, right? Like an infectious disease type of thing (laughs). We don't want that. So, we want it to be directed in a positive way."

That's the issue. Skattebo has one speed. Full throttle. Joel Corry, a former NFL agent, believes Skattebo needs to be reined in. If the Giants won't do it, maybe his agent, or reps, should.

When situations like these arise, an agent should provide counsel to their client. It's an agent's job to tell a client what he needs to hear, not what he wants to hear. That isn't always done. Some agents are reluctant to be candid for fear of being fired and instead become enablers.

The initial backflip created an opportunity to warn Skattebo about the risk he was taking, considering he hadn't completely recovered from a serious injury. Had there been a major setback that jeopardized or ended Skattebo's 2026 season, which fortunately didn't occur with either backflip, he would have landed on the Reserve/Non-Football Injury list (NFI).

Corry is referring to the backflip Skattebo performed earlier this year at Fanatics Fest, where he didn't stick the landing. For a player who had not shown he could play football yet with his reconstructed ankle, this opened a lot of eyes. Not in a good way, either.

The Giants are aware they can't corral Skattebo completely. His persona is what it is. He's reckless in every direction he goes, so they had to go out and get themselves some insurance.

In free agency this year, they signed Pro Bowl fullback Patrick Ricard to lead the way out of the backfield. Ricard will take on the tacklers that Skattebo was taking head-on. It should free up some running room and spare Skattebo some wear and tear.

Then the Giants signed 232-pound Najee Harris to take early snaps and soften up the defense. That was Skattebo's job. Was.

Skattebo is talking about having a 2,000-yard season. That will happen maybe if he averages 20 yards per carry. His workload will be managed to the point where he might get anywhere from eight to 12 carries per game, max.

With Harris in tow and the team still very much aware that Tyrone Tracy Jr. is their only back with any measurable speed, Skattebo is in a committee situation with the Giants. Let's not leave out Devin Singletary, who is on the roster to provide a quick change-up a half-dozen times a game.

Skattebo may not want to pace himself and change, so the Giants could be quietly doing it for him.

title: “There are Survivors in Football”: Shannon Sharpe Calls Out Cam Skattebo After Giants RB’s Retirement Admission

fullText:
On Thursday, Cam Skattebo admitted that he had considered retirement a month into his ankle injury last year. This was just a few months into his NFL career, with the former Arizona State running back having been drafted by the New York Giants in 2025.

The admission came in an interview earlier this week in 'Up&Adams' in which the running back spoke about a promise he made to himself in college regarding retiring at the first sign of serious injury. Skattebo also spoke about how the injury allowed him to get to know himself better.

This candid moment by Skattebo caught some by surprise, including Hall of Famer Shannon Sharpe, who was taken aback by the idea that a single injury could take such a toll on a player's confidence. He said as much on Friday's edition of 'Nightcap':

"There are no winners in football; there are survivors in football. You play probably the sports that the most serious injuries happen… You gotta know when the journey is over," said Sharpe

Sharpe and his co-hosts, former NFL player Chad Johnson and former NBA player Joe Johnson, were surprised by the idea that a young player would contemplate retirement shortly after their debut. They saw it as a failure of mentality, at a moment when Skattebo should've been focused on returning to the field with the New York Giants.

Speaking on Thursday in Up&Adams, Cam Skattebo explained that he briefly considered leaving the NFL after his serious ankle injury last year. For him, it was all down to a promise he made to himself before making the jump to the pros. He wouldn't let the NFL get in the way of his health:

"Coming out of college and going into the NFL, I think I gave myself one rule and it was if I ever got a major injury I was done playing," he said. "And that happened seven games into my career, so it kind of sucked."

He also explained that in the end, the recovery process allowed him to get to know himself better:

"Just finding who I was, finding my happiness, finding the person I wanted to be on and off the field. And I think that's something I built over the last nine, 10 months and being able to now focus back on football,"

Nonetheless, Cam Skattebo did say that the recovery process did take a heavy mental toll on him, with days in which he would spend up to 14 hours doing absolutely nothing.
